theory.title: Emotion, regulation and psychological flexibility
theory.explanation: Develop precise language for emotional literacy, triggers, reappraisal, distress tolerance and adaptive coping. Distinguish acknowledging an emotion from acting on its first impulse.
theory.tip: Avoid presenting emotional regulation as constant calm or suppression. Generated audio remains pending review.

reading.english:
Regulation Rather Than Suppression

Emotional self-regulation is sometimes mistaken for the ability to remain calm at all times. In practice, it involves recognising an emotional response, understanding what may have triggered it and choosing how to act. The aim is not to suppress every uncomfortable feeling. Emotions can provide useful information about needs, expectations and perceived threats, even when the first interpretation is incomplete.

One strategy is cognitive reappraisal: reconsidering the meaning of a situation before responding. A delayed reply, for instance, may be interpreted as rejection, although there may be several less personal explanations. Pausing can create room to test the initial assumption and select a measured response. This does not guarantee that distress will disappear; it may simply prevent an automatic reaction from escalating a conflict.

Effective regulation also depends on context. Sleep, workload, social support and previous experiences can affect a person's capacity to manage frustration. Mindfulness and self-compassion may help some people notice emotions without being overwhelmed by them. However, no single technique works in every circumstance. Psychological flexibility involves adapting strategies, recognising limits and seeking support when necessary.
reading.spanish: Regularse en lugar de suprimir. El texto explica la reevaluación cognitiva, la influencia del contexto y la flexibilidad psicológica.
